I was reading the survey results when the CEO called.
While we were preparing the town hall, the news leaked.
At nine in the morning everybody was talking about it.
People were not working that afternoon. They were waiting.
Viviane, I have a question I never asked you. What was happening here the week we announced the deal?
Honestly? The rumor was already in the stores. People were talking about it two weeks before the announcement.
Two weeks? We thought it was confidential.
It never is. While we were preparing the town hall, three store managers called me to ask if they were losing their jobs.
And what were you telling them at that point?
Sorry, could you say that again, please?
At that point, what were you telling people?
The truth: that I did not know yet. And then I ran a town hall every Friday for two months. Morale was low, but nobody was inventing stories any more.
That is why we kept your team. Most companies lose half of it in a transition.
At ten in the morning nobody was working.
People were waiting for us to say something.
So I ran a town hall every Friday for two months.

It was a Tuesday, and I remember it minute by minute. At eight in the morning I was in a meeting about the training calendar, which now sounds ridiculous. At eight thirty my phone started ringing and it did not stop. At nine the CEO sent the email to the whole company. I was standing in the corridor when I read it, and I read it twice, because the first time I did not understand anything. By ten o clock nobody was working. People were standing in small groups, everybody was asking the same question, and nobody had an answer, including me. The hardest part was not the news. It was the four days after it, when we knew nothing and people were waiting for us to say something. I learned one thing that week. In a change, people can accept bad news. What they cannot accept is silence.

Tell me about a difficult change you went through. I ask that in almost every interview, and the answers split into two groups. In the first group, everything happens to the person. The company was sold, my manager left, the team was reduced, it was very hard. Every verb is about them, and the person is never doing anything. In the second group, the story has the same problems, but somewhere in the middle the person says: so I did this. I ran a meeting every week. I called the twelve people who were most at risk. I wrote the document nobody asked for. Same change, completely different candidate. And I am not looking for a hero. Half of those decisions did not even work. I am looking for somebody who was acting and not only waiting, because that is exactly what I am going to need from them here.

At eight I was sitting in a meeting about the training calendar. At eight thirty three store managers were calling me about a rumor. I was standing in the corridor when I read the CEO email. By ten o clock nobody was working.
